MA3491 overview

MA3491 Topic Guide

Coding Bounds and Block-Code Parameters

Turn a code question into q, n, M and d before choosing a bound.

Purpose

Bounds say what size a q-ary code can possibly have, and let you recognise perfect and MDS cases.Exam use: q,n,M,d,t, ball volume, integer rounding and comparison/interpretation of bounds are shown.

Question plan

  1. State q, length n, size M and minimum distance d.
  2. Choose Singleton for a general size bound; choose sphere packing when error correction matters.
  3. Substitute carefully, then interpret equality.
  4. Question interpretation: Extract q,n,M,d first; decide whether the question asks an upper bound, existence, or perfect packing before selecting Singleton, Hamming or Gilbert-Varshamov.

Formulas

For C⊆Fq n, |C|=M: Singleton: M≤qn−d+1. If t=⌊(d−1)/2⌋, sphere packing: M∑i=0 t(n choose i)(q−1)i≤qn.Rapid recall: Singleton: M<=q^{n-d+1}; Hamming with t=floor((d-1)/2): M sum_{i=0}^t C(n,i)(q-1)^i <= q^n; equality means perfect packing.

Derivation

Delete d−1 coordinates. No two codewords can become equal, or their original distance would be at most d−1; there are qn−d+1 remaining words. For sphere packing, radius-t balls about codewords are disjoint, so their total size fits in Fq n.Exam workflow: Compute t carefully, write the ball volume, substitute all parameters, and round an upper bound down only at the final integer step.

Worked example

A binary (n=7,M=16,d=3) code has t=1. Sphere packing gives 16(1+7)=128=27, so it is perfect. Singleton gives 16≤25.

Medium/hard paper-style synthesis

For a binary (n=7,d=3) code, t=1 and a Hamming ball has volume C(7,0)+C(7,1)=8. Therefore M*8<=2^7=128, so M<=16. The [7,4,3] Hamming code has M=2^4=16 and meets equality, hence is perfect. Singleton only gives M<=2^5=32 and is weaker here.

Graduated exam bridge

1. Apply Singleton to a ternary (5,M,3) code. Check: M≤33=27.

2. Prove the Singleton bound, then decide whether a binary (5,4,3) code is perfect. Check: write the puncturing argument; t=1 gives 4(1+5)=24≠32, so not perfect.

Hard paper-style synthesis

Paper-style synthesis: bound a ternary length-6 code with d=3. Check t=1, ball volume 1+6(3-1)=13, so M<=floor(3^6/13)=56; Singleton gives M<=3^4=81, so Hamming is stronger.

Practice question - choose and apply a bound [8 marks]

Inspired by: MA3491 2024/25 Q1(a-b). Task. Bound the size M of a ternary length-6 code with minimum distance 3 using sphere packing and Singleton, and say which is stronger. [8 marks]

Demand diagnosis and fastest route: d=3 gives t=1; calculate the q-ary ball volume before comparing numerical bounds.

Worked answer: A radius-one ball has volume V3(6,1)=C(6,0)+C(6,1)(3-1)=1+12=13. Sphere packing gives 13M≤36=729, so M≤floor(729/13)=56. Singleton gives M≤qn-d+1=34=81. Hence the sphere-packing bound is stronger here because 56<81.

Topic-specific trap: t is floor((d-1)/2), not d-1.

Mistakes

  • Using d rather than t in the ball radius.
  • Calling equality in Singleton “perfect”; it means MDS.
  • Forgetting (q−1)i.
  • Recovery rule: Use t=floor((d-1)/2), not d-1; otherwise the Hamming balls correspond to a decoding radius the code cannot guarantee.

Checklist

  • I can identify all four parameters.
  • I can explain why balls are disjoint.
  • I state what equality means.
  • Final 60-second audit: q,n,M,d,t, ball volume, integer rounding and comparison/interpretation of bounds are shown.
